"title": "Major concerns with the integrity of the mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier in dodecyl-phosphocholine used for solution NMR studies",

"executive_summary": "This paper serves as a rigorous critique of a study by Brüschweiler et al. regarding the refolding of the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier (AAC3) using the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC). The authors argue that DPC causes immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3, rendering subsequent NMR and ITC data biologically irrelevant. They present direct evidence from thermostability assays showing that AAC3 in DPC lacks a melting transition, unlike the protein in mild detergents like dodecyl-maltoside. Furthermore, they highlight discrepancies in binding affinities, noting that reported Kd values for the inhibitor CATR in DPC (~15 µM) are three to four orders of magnitude higher than the consensus low nanomolar range observed in native membranes. The authors also point out a typographical error in a cited reference where a Kd was listed in µM instead of nM, further undermining the validity of the comparative data. Ultimately, the paper concludes that the dynamic studies and structural interpretations based on DPC-refolded protein are flawed because the protein exists in a non-native, unfolded state.",

summary.title: Major concerns with the integrity of the mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier in dodecyl-phosphocholine used for solution NMR studies
summary.authors: Martin S King; Paul G Crichton; Jonathan J Ruprecht; Edmund R S Kunji
summary.executive_summary: This paper serves as a rigorous critique of a study by Brüschweiler et al. regarding the refolding of the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier (AAC3) using the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC). The authors argue that DPC causes immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3, rendering subsequent NMR and ITC data biologically irrelevant. They present direct evidence from thermostability assays showing that AAC3 in DPC lacks a melting transition, unlike the protein in mild detergents like dodecyl-maltoside. Furthermore, they highlight discrepancies in binding affinities, noting that reported Kd values for the inhibitor CATR in DPC (~15 µM) are three to four orders of magnitude higher than the consensus low nanomolar range observed in native membranes. The authors also point out a typographical error in a cited reference where a Kd was listed in µM instead of nM, further undermining the validity of the comparative data. Ultimately, the paper concludes that the dynamic studies and structural interpretations based on DPC-refolded protein are flawed because the protein exists in a non-native, unfolded state.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper serves as a rigorous critique of a study by Brüschweiler et al. regarding the refolding of the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier (AAC3) using the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC). The authors argue that DPC causes immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3, rendering subsequent NMR and ITC data biologically irrelevant. They present direct evidence from thermostability assays showing that AAC3 in DPC lacks a melting transition, unlike the protein in mild detergents like dodecyl-maltoside. Furthermore, they highlight discrepancies in binding affinities, noting that reported Kd values for the inhibitor CATR in DPC (~15 µM) are three to four orders of magnitude higher than the consensus low nanomolar range observed in native membranes. The authors also point out a typographical error in a cited reference where a Kd was listed in µM instead of nM, further undermining the validity of the comparative data. Ultimately, the paper concludes that the dynamic studies and structural interpretations based on DPC-refolded protein are flawed because the protein exists in a non-native, unfolded state.

Research Context
The yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier AAC3 is a well-studied membrane protein. Its structure has been solved by electron and x--ray crystallography. Interactions with inhibitors atractyloside (ATR) and carboxyatractyloside (CATR) were previously characterized. A recent study claimed AAC3 could be refolded to homogeneity from inclusion bodies using DPC. The claim suggests AAC3 remains folded and active during ITC and NMR experiments.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether DPC preserves the native structure and function of AAC3. The authors hypothesize that DPC denatures AAC3 rather than maintaining its folded state. It is predicted that binding affinities measured in DPC will be significantly lower than in native membranes. The study aims to demonstrate that functional assays are missing to verify activity. The authors predict that thermostability profiles will differ between DPC and mild detergents.

Methodological Details
The study focuses on the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier AAC3. Protein was isolated from the inner membrane of mitochondria where it was folded and active. The authors used ITC to measure a Kd of ~15 µM for CATR binding to DPC--refolded AAC3. Published Kd values for CATR binding to AAC in the membrane are all in the low nanomolar range. Native AAC3 from yeast mitochondria purified in dodecyl-maltoside/tetraoleoyl cardiolipin gave an average Kd of 72 nM. Thermostability assays used the thiol--reactive fluorophore N--[4--(7--diethylamino--4--methyl--3--coumarinyl)phenyl] maleimide (CPM). Fluorescence was measured on a Qiagen Rotorgene Q using the HRM channel. Measurements were made in 1 °C intervals from 25 - 90 °C with a ramp rate of 5.6 °C/min. Reconstitution involved mixing L--α--phosphatidylcholine and tetraoleoyl cardiolipin in a 20:1 (w/w) ratio. ADP uptake assays used a Hamilton MicroLab Star robot with a MultiScreenHTS--HA 96--well filter plate. Transport was stopped at 0, 10, 20, 30, 45 s, 1, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10 and 15 min.

Procedures And Architectures
The authors claim DPC leads to immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation. The study notes that the µM unit used in a reference was a typographical error corrected to 192 nM. Published Kd values for CATR binding to AAC in the membrane are all in the low nanomolar range. ADP transport by AAC3 is half--maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR. The Kd of ADP binding determined by NMR (500 μM) is ~85--fold higher than published consensus values. AAC3 has an isoelectric point of 9.82, meaning it is highly positively charged. CATR and substrates ADP and ATP are negatively charged molecules at neutral pH. The ring of transmembrane α-helices is held together largely by the lateral pressure of the membrane. Binding of CATR introduces a large number of polar and van der Waals interactions. The experiments reported here and elsewhere clearly show that the Kd of CATR binding to the folded mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier is in the low nanomolar range. To obtain the crystal structure, AAC3 was first inhibited with CATR in the mitochondrial membrane. A clear interpretable density for CATR could be observed after solubilization and crystallization. The protein concentration was approximately 1 μM AAC3 in thermostability assays. Particulate material was removed by ultracentrifugation (140,000 g, 45 min, 4 °C). The soluble fraction was loaded onto a Ni--Sepharose high performance column at 1 mL min --1. The column was washed with buffer containing 20 mM PIPES pH 7.0, 150 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole, 0.1% dodecyl--maltoside, 0.1 mg mL --1 tetraoleoyl cardiolipin. The column material was resuspended with 5 mM CaCl2 and 75 μL Factor Xa. The cleaved protein was separated from the nickel sepharose media using filtration and centrifugation. The protein was snap--frozen and stored in liquid nitrogen. A 5 mg mL --1 stock of CPM dissolved in DMSO was diluted 50--fold into buffer. Approximately 1.5 μg of purified protein was added into a final volume of 45 μL buffer. Carboxyatractyloside (500 μM stock) was titrated into purified 25 μM AAC3. The purified protein was either added directly to the lipid/detergent reconstitution mix or diluted 20--fold. The detergent was stepwise removed from the reconstitution mix through addition of 4 × 30 mg and 4 × 60 mg of Bio--Beads SM--2. The resulting proteoliposome suspension was separated from the biobeads using an empty spin column. The proteoliposomes were eluted in 1.5 mL and diluted a further 9--fold in external buffer. Uptake of radiolabeled ADP was initiated by the addition of 100 μL of external buffer containing [ 14 C]--ADP (2.2 GBq mmol -1 ).

Key Results
The presence of DPC leads to immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3. The consensus Kd values for CATR binding are at least three to four orders of magnitude lower than those in DPC. Our ITC measurements using native AAC3 from yeast mitochondria gave an average Kd of 72 nM. The Kd of 72 nM is 200 to 2000--fold lower than those reported in Brüschweiler et al.. Only 2 out of 10 trials succeeded in measuring the enthalpic change for native AAC3. When diluted into 3 mM DPC, a high signal was observed with no transition, showing AAC3 is in a non--native state. CATR addition had no effect in DPC, demonstrating there was no functional binding site. Dilution of AAC3 into DPC before reconstitution resulted in a complete loss of CATR--sensitive ADP uptake in liposomes. The Kd of ADP binding determined by NMR (500 μM) is ~85--fold higher than published consensus values. Residues assigned to have chemical shift perturbations induced by ADP are largely on the matrix side. The chemical shift perturbations could represent non--specific interactions of CATR or ADP with AAC3. CATR binding should lock the protein in a non--dynamic aborted state. The observed dynamics in the presence of substrate do not provide a plausible structural mechanism for transport. DPC is harsh enough to solubilise unfolded mitochondrial carrier protein from E. coli inclusion bodies. DPC is able to denature functional well--folded carrier protein prepared in mild non--ionic detergents. In thermostability assays, AAC3 purified from yeast mitochondrial membranes displayed a typical protein melt curve in dodecyl--maltoside. When CATR was added at a molar ratio of one or above, a marked shift in stability of AAC3 to higher temperatures is observed. The data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The ring of transmembrane α-helices is held together largely by the lateral pressure of the membrane. Unliganded AAC3 in detergent micelles is prone to unfolding due to lack of membrane pressure. Binding of CATR introduces a large number of polar and van der Waals interactions. These interactions explain the high affinity of CATR for AAC3 as well as the improved stability in detergents. The experiments reported here and elsewhere clearly show that the Kd of CATR binding to the folded mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier is in the low nanomolar range. This is consistent with its role as a powerful toxin. The extremely low affinity of CATR to refolded AAC3 in DPC begs the question whether the binding is specific at all. Only a limited number of chemical shift perturbations for CATR binding to refolded AAC3 are observed. All of them are dynamic, which is inconsistent with tight binding. These residues are not near the known CATR binding site nor are they on structural elements that are involved in CATR binding. The Kd of ADP binding determined by NMR (500 μM) is ~85--fold higher than the published consensus values. Residues assigned to have chemical shift perturbations induced by ADP are largely on the matrix side of the carrier. These residues are far away from the consensus binding site in the central cavity. The chemical shift perturbations could represent non--specific interactions of CATR or ADP with AAC3. CATR binding should lock the protein in a non--dynamic aborted state. The observed dynamics in the presence of substrate do not provide a plausible structural mechanism for transport. DPC is harsh enough to solubilise unfolded mitochondrial carrier protein from E. coli inclusion bodies. DPC is able to denature functional well--folded carrier protein prepared in mild non--ionic detergents. In conclusion, we believe that the data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors note that the µM unit used in a reference was a typographical error corrected to 192 nM. Published Kd values for CATR binding to AAC in the membrane are all in the low nanomolar range. Our ITC measurements using native AAC3 from yeast mitochondria gave an average Kd of 72 nM. The Kd of 72 nM is 200 to 2000--fold lower than those reported in Brüschweiler et al.. These experiments were very difficult to do (only 2 out of 10 trials succeeded). When diluted into 3 mM DPC, a high signal was observed with no transition, showing AAC3 is in a non--native state. CATR addition had no effect in DPC, demonstrating there was no functional binding site. Dilution of AAC3 into DPC before reconstitution resulted in a complete loss of CATR--sensitive ADP uptake in liposomes. The Kd of ADP binding determined by NMR (500 μM) is ~85--fold higher than the published consensus values. Residues assigned to have chemical shift perturbations induced by ADP are largely on the matrix side of the carrier. These residues are far away from the consensus binding site in the central cavity. The chemical shift perturbations could represent non--specific interactions of CATR or ADP with AAC3. CATR binding should lock the protein in a non--dynamic aborted state. The observed dynamics in the presence of substrate do not provide a plausible structural mechanism for transport. DPC is harsh enough to solubilise unfolded mitochondrial carrier protein from E. coli inclusion bodies. DPC is able to denature functional well--folded carrier protein prepared in mild non--ionic detergents. In conclusion, we believe that the data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance.

Claims
DPC causes immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3. The presence of DPC leads to immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3. When diluted into 3 mM DPC, a high signal was observed with no transition. CATR addition had no effect in DPC, demonstrating there was no functional binding site. The authors claim AAC3 can be refolded to homogeneity from inclusion bodies using DPC. The authors claim AAC3 is maintained in a folded and active state for the duration of ITC and NMR experiments. The data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance. The extremely low affinity of CATR to refolded AAC3 in DPC begs the question whether the binding is specific at all.
Binding affinities in DPC are significantly lower than in native membranes. Thus, the consensus is at least three to four orders of magnitude lower than the Kd values reported for refolded AAC3 in DPC 1. Our ITC measurements using native AAC3 from yeast mitochondria gave an average Kd of 72 nM. The Kd of 72 nM is 200 to 2000--fold lower than those reported in Brüschweiler et al.. The authors used ITC to measure a Kd of ~15 µM for the binding of CATR to DPC--refolded AAC3. The experiments reported here and elsewhere clearly show that the Kd of CATR binding to the folded mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier is in the low nanomolar range.
NMR data may reflect non-specific interactions rather than specific binding. The chemical shift perturbations could represent non--specific interactions of CATR or ADP with AAC3. Residues assigned to have chemical shift perturbations induced by ADP are largely on the matrix side of the carrier. These residues are far away from the consensus binding site in the central cavity. The authors determined CATR--dependent chemical shift perturbations by NMR, giving a Kd of ~150 µM. Only a limited number of chemical shift perturbations for CATR binding to refolded AAC3 are observed.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Only 2 out of 10 trials succeeded in measuring the enthalpic change for native AAC3. Dilution of AAC3 into DPC before reconstitution resulted in a complete loss of CATR--sensitive ADP uptake in liposomes.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows that ADP transport by AAC3 is half--maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR. Figure 1b shows that native AAC3 from yeast mitochondria gave an average Kd of 72 nM. Figure 1c shows that AAC3 purified from yeast mitochondrial membranes displayed a typical protein melt curve in dodecyl--maltoside. Figure 1d shows that when diluted into 3 mM DPC, a high signal was observed with no transition. Supplementary Fig. 2 shows that dilution of AAC3 into DPC before reconstitution resulted in a complete loss of CATR--sensitive ADP uptake.

Three Takeaways
1. DPC causes immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3. 2. The consensus Kd values for CATR binding are at least three to four orders of magnitude lower than those in DPC. 3. The data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance.
